prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in poetry, that builds from memory, the body and dream an inner cosmos of metaphysical scope and exceptional formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B050, a single writer, in one prize part. What I have tightened is the scope of the citation and the evidence it rests on. The merit case is distinctiveness of voice, formal architecture and imaginative depth across a body of work. As publicly described, the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding) and Solenoid build memory, the body and dream into one metaphysical project, with long, densely patterned sentences and large structures whose recurring images give them an internal logic. The poetic origin and the essays suggest the prose grew from a wider literary practice, so the claim does not rest on one celebrated book. In answer to the chair question about which works each member relies on, I rely mainly on Orbitor/Blinding and Solenoid. I treat the poetry and essays as supporting context, because my knowledge of them is thinner. For that reason the citation leads with the prose and mentions poetry only as its root, so it claims no more than the evidence bears. I would also say that unanimity in round 1 is not evidence of merit. The case has to survive the open questions about translation and late-volume repetition on its own terms. I have not found a merit reason to prefer no award (P000). The reservations concern how securely the committee can document the work, not whether it is of high literary order. I keep B009 (Zurita) as my first alternative and B018 (Tawada) as my second. My assessments rest on public knowledge, not fresh reading or independent verification.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. A judgment of density, rhythm and long sentence architecture depends on translation, and the poetry, essays and early work are the thinnest part of my coverage, so the whole-oeuvre claim is partly inferred from the large novels. The second reservation is whether the late, very large volumes deepen the project or enlarge it by repeating motifs. No colleague has offered close-reading evidence either way, and I have none. If the committee found that the later books enclose the earlier project instead of developing it, the sustained-quality criterion would be weaker and the citation would have to narrow to the major cycles. There is also a risk that my own move from Zurita to Cărtărescu reflects the shape of the evidence available to me (prose architecture survives translation better than verse) and not a real difference in literary achievement. I cannot rule that out, which is why B009 stays a serious alternative.

responses.point: Sward calls the repetition worry the most serious qualification on her own first choice and argues for judging the cycles as a whole, not the late volumes alone. She also says she would treat Zurita as a leading alternative if the written sequences can be shown to stand on their own in the original, and she asks what would show that Tawada's shorter forms sustain depth.
responses.response: I agree that the cycles should be judged as wholes, and I will apply that to my own choice. The Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid should be read as architectures, and the question is whether Solenoid develops the earlier project or only extends its machinery. On Zurita, I accept your condition. The citation would have to name the written sequences, with Purgatory and Anteparadise as the core, and exclude the landscape interventions. On Tawada, I can name what I would need: evidence that the estrangement between Japanese and German does more than recur from book to book, and that it develops across the novels, essays and poetry as one authorship. Until the committee has that, I keep her as a second alternative and not a first choice. I cannot supply it from public knowledge, and I will not pretend to.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says the committee should test directly whether excess and encyclopedic scale reads as sustained imaginative depth or as lack of selection. He adds that agreement in the opening rankings is not evidence of merit, and that Zurita's cycle should be tested by comparing individual poems, not the scale of the project.
responses.response: I accept both points and apply them to myself. My move to B050 in round 1 should not be read as a result of the shared ranking, and I do not rest it on that. On the test you propose, a poem-by-poem comparison is the right standard for Zurita, and I admit that I cannot carry it out in Spanish from the translated corpus. That asymmetry between what I can judge and what I suspect is the reason B009 is my alternative and not my first choice. For Cărtărescu the parallel test is whether passages and volumes differ in kind or only in length. I have no verified answer, and I would rather record that openly than claim one.

responses.point: Mattson keeps NDiaye as an alternative and not her preferred laureate. She grants that the oeuvre is more compact than Cărtărescu's, and she says that the length of the volumes is an argument for reading the whole corpus before treating the novels as the oeuvre.
responses.response: Your last point is the one I most want to carry into the vote, and it is why I have narrowed my citation to what I can support. I do not rank NDiaye in my alternatives. That is a judgment about my own coverage and about cumulative weight, not about the quality of the control and the uncanny tone you describe. I ranked her sixth for the same reason you and others name, the question of breadth against the largest bodies of work. If you can say which works carry her claim across decades, as the round-1 questions ask, I would listen. I would want a case that her later work deepens the early fiction and does not only repeat its method.

responses.point: Palm argues that the loss in translation is less total for large-scale prose architecture than for poetry built on sonic and sequential effects. She also says Zurita's case depends more on historical context than Cărtărescu's, and she wants the two kept separate.
responses.response: I agree with the translation asymmetry, and it is part of why I weigh the two differently now. But the asymmetry is an evidentiary point, not a literary one, and I should not let it grow into a judgment that prose is worth more than verse. If the committee had dependable Spanish readers, or the anonymous regional expert reports, they could correct my view and would count for more than my judgment. On historical context, I agree the sequences must show force beyond their occasion. I think the written work does in part, but I cannot demonstrate it from translation. That is why I hold him as an alternative and do not move him up.

responses.point: Carlberg argues that the committee should say which volumes it relies on, and that this is a better answer to the density and consensus problem than preferring a body of work that is harder to read in translation. She also sees Adonis as an achievement concerning a whole literary language.
responses.response: I accept your suggestion, and the citation above is my attempt to follow it: it rests on the prose, with poetry named as a root only. On Adonis, I ranked him last in my opening because the renewal of Arabic poetic form is exactly what I cannot judge through translation, and I have not changed that view. I agree with you that the linguistic significance is large and that his political positions are context, not literary evidence. I would not name him among my two alternatives without a reliable Arabic-language reading of the poems, and I think the committee should reserve his case until it has one.

uncertainties: How much of the syntactic and rhythmic design of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives in the translations the committee actually uses. I cannot answer the chair's question about this myself, and the supplied evidence contains no Romanian-language reading or regional expert report.
Whether the late, very large volumes deepen the project or repeat its motifs. No member has offered verified close-reading evidence, and I have none.
Whether the poetry, essays and early work support a whole-oeuvre claim as strongly as the novels, given that my coverage of them is thinner and the citation is partly inferred from the major cycles.

For Zurita, whether the written sequences carry the case on their own in Spanish, apart from the landscape interventions and the historical occasion, and how strictly the citation can be limited to the poems.
For Tawada, whether the Japanese and German bodies of work together show sustained depth across short and episodic forms, given uneven translation of wordplay.
All of my assessments rest on public knowledge of representative works, not on fresh reading or independent verification, and my view of the full bibliographies may be incomplete.
This is a simulated committee recommendation, not the decision of the full Swedish Academy, and Carlberg's actual voting status is undocumented, so her simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from the supplied profile, and I request no recusal. Disclosure carried over from round 1: my opening ranking placed Zurita (B009) first and Cărtărescu (B050) second, and I moved B050 to first in round 1 on the merit arguments, not on the number of colleagues ranking it. In round 2 I keep B050 and keep B009 as my first alternative. My scholarly work on modern poetry, the fragment, nihilism, exile literature, and my translation of Paul Celan, is context only and not evidence of a connection to any shortlisted writer or of a preference for poetry candidates. I also chair the committee and was the author of the round-1 chair summary, so the questions it frames reflect my selection, and I have tried to answer them on the same terms as any member.
